mainEntity.name: What are the main composition rules in photography?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Commonly taught composition techniques include the rule of

thirds, leading lines, symmetry, patterns, framing, balance

and negative space. Each gives you an arrangement to explore.

Choose according to what you want the photograph to express,

then judge the effect in the actual image.

mainEntity.name: What are the seven rules of composition?

acceptedAnswer.text:
There is no single agreed list of seven composition rules.

One common selection is thirds, leading lines, framing,

symmetry, balance, negative space and repetition. Different

guides group these techniques differently. Learning how

they affect your photographs is more useful than memorising

a particular list.

mainEntity.name: Which composition rule should a beginner learn first?

acceptedAnswer.text:
The rule of thirds is an accessible placement exercise.

Begin by noticing what interests you, then compare placing

it near a thirds line with placing it centrally. Look at

how the surrounding space and relationships change.

Explain which version better supports your intention.

mainEntity.name: Does a subject always need to be off-centre?

acceptedAnswer.text:
No. Central placement can support symmetry, directness or

stillness. Off-centre placement changes the space around

an element and its relationship with the rest of the frame.

Try both where practical and compare their effect.

Lesson

27 — Framing explores these choices further.

mainEntity.name: Should I fill the frame or leave negative space?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Choose according to what the surroundings contribute.

A tight frame may emphasise detail or gesture. More space

may express scale, isolation, stillness or context.

Compare both versions rather than aiming for a fixed

proportion. See

Lesson

30 — Negative Space for more examples of this decision.

mainEntity.name: Do leading lines have to point towards the main subject?

acceptedAnswer.text:
No. A line may connect areas of the photograph, suggest

depth, disappear into the distance or continue beyond

the frame. Consider what that movement contributes to

the image. In

Lesson

29 — Leading Lines , visual pathways also include

connections created by light, colour and repeated shapes.

mainEntity.name: Does every photograph need to look balanced?

acceptedAnswer.text:
A photograph can work through stability, tension or

deliberate dominance. Look at how attention is distributed

and whether that relationship supports your intention.

Adding another element simply to equalise the frame

may weaken it. Explore this in

Lesson

32 — Compositional Balance .

mainEntity.name: How can I improve my photography composition?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Photograph one scene in two ways, changing one compositional

choice. Compare what each version communicates and identify

visible reasons for your preference. Ask another viewer

what they notice, then decide what to test next.

Lesson

34 — Improving Composition develops this review process.

mainEntity.name: Can cropping improve a photograph’s composition?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Cropping can change the frame’s boundaries, proportions

and relationships. Compare a proposed crop with the

original and check what it removes. Keep it when it

strengthens the photograph’s meaning or feeling.

Cropping cannot recover anything outside the original frame.

mainEntity.name: How do I know when to break a composition rule?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Compare the suggested arrangement with an alternative.

If central placement, extra space or an uneven distribution

of attention better expresses your intention, use it.

Explain the choice through its effect on the photograph.

The

Photography

Composition Framework connects these decisions through

SEE → FEEL → TECHNIQUE.
